evidence.claim: San Bernardo was one of four communities founded by Canarians who arrived in Spanish Louisiana between 1778 and 1783.
evidence.quote: Between 1778 and 1783 another 2,100 Canarians arrived in Spanish Louisiana and founded the four communities of Galveztown, Valenzuela, Barataria, and San Bernardo.

evidence.claim: The community preserved much of its language and culture into the 21st century.
evidence.quote: the community of San Bernardo (Saint Bernard) was able to preserve much of its unique culture and language into the 21st century.

evidence.claim: The Spanish dialect brought from the Canary Islands is still spoken in St. Bernard Parish.
evidence.quote: The dialect of Spanish spoken in the Canary Islands during the 18th century was still spoken by older Isleños until the 1950s in San Antonio but is still spoken in St. Bernard Parish.

evidence.claim: Hotel dishes unearthed during swimming-pool excavations tell an unexpected part of Arabi’s stockyard history: table scraps from New Orleans hotels and restaurants once fed the animals here.
evidence.quote: When excavation for swimming pools was done, residents found dishes from New Orleans hotels and restaurants whose table scraps were once used to feed animals.

evidence.claim: The settlement began as Stockyard Landing, named for its stockyards and slaughterhouses.
evidence.quote: Arabi began as the community known as Stockyard Landing, because of the many stockyards and slaughterhouses located there.

evidence.claim: Those businesses also helped redraw the parish boundary.
evidence.quote: Business interests of the stockyards wanted to be free from control of New Orleans

evidence.claim: Seeking independence from New Orleans control, stockyard interests persuaded Louisiana to transfer the area downriver from Jackson Barracks to St. Bernard Parish in 1875.
evidence.quote: Business interests of the stockyards wanted to be free from control of New Orleans and persuaded the state of Louisiana to transfer dominion of the area downriver from Jackson Barracks to St. Bernard Parish in 1875.

evidence.claim: Chalmette preserves the site where Andrew Jackson’s forces defeated the British in January 1815.

evidence.claim: Fazendeville, an African American community with stores, a school and the Battle Ground Baptist Church, later occupied land here.
evidence.quote: As it matured, the self-contained village of Fazendeville grew to have its own general stores, a one-room schoolhouse which taught first through eighth grades, two benevolent societies, and the Battle Ground Baptist Church.

evidence.claim: In 1964, the parish government expropriated the land for park expansion.
evidence.quote: The community ended in 1964 when the St. Bernard Parish Government expropriated the rights to the land for expansion of the park around the battlefield site.

evidence.claim: More than 50 families were forced to relocate when the National Park Service acquired it; demolition was completed in 1966.
evidence.quote: More than 50 families were forced to relocate when the National Park Service obtained the land. Fazendeville Road was closed on November 25, 1964, and the demolition of Fazendeville was completed in 1966.
